description: We’re building for more than a challenge. We want to use technology, science, and innovation to help humanity understand and shape a better future. I’m passionate about space, robotics, physics, and engineering, and I’m looking for people who are highly skilled, curious, and ready to give their all. Developers, AI/ML, data scientists, GIS experts, engineers, and designers are welcome.
summary:
During the 2026 monsoon, open water at Tonlé Sap in Cambodia expanded from 1,043 km² to 1,572 km². We built Dancing Earth, an open-source web app, so anyone can follow changes like this on a map and hear them as music.

The app uses L-band radar from the NASA-ISRO NISAR satellite. Radar can see through clouds and smoke. The app lets you compare each radar image with an optical photo taken the same day. On 29 of the 77 days NISAR passed over our five places, the photo showed mostly clouds.

You can pick a date on a timeline, drag a slider between two images and see where things changed on a colour-coded map. A single sentence tells you what changed and by how much. You can also play the image as music. Brighter areas produce higher notes, and places that changed more sound louder.

Water is our main focus, but the app also tracks wildfires, forest clearing and farm fields. For the Shingle Fire in Oregon, 96% of the vegetation loss we detected lies within the official fire perimeter.

Scientists can download the measurements as CSV, and each place comes with a short story for teachers and students.
details:
What it does. Dancing Earth shows surface change at five places using NISAR L2 GCOV radar data: Tonlé Sap lake in Cambodia (flood), the Shingle Fire and Big Grass Fire in Oregon (wildfires), Rondônia in Brazil (forest clearing) and California's Central Valley (farm fields). For each place the user can switch between HH, HV and a Change layer, drag a before/after slider, compare the radar with a camera photo of the same day (Optical layer), play a timeline of all satellite passes, click any spot to get its own time series, download the data as CSV, and copy a link that reopens the exact view.

Live world. A world map shows natural events that NASA EONET is tracking right now. Clicking an event, or any place on land, loads the newest NISAR quick-look radar image of that spot directly from NASA's archive in the browser, with earlier passes to compare and an estimate of the next pass.

How it works. A Python script searches the ASF archive, reads only a small window of each 1.8 GB file over the internet, averages the signal in linear power and saves small images and statistics. The change map compares each pass with a reference (for fires: the average of all passes before the fire) after smoothing to reduce speckle. Open water is mapped from HV, because wind makes water bright in HH. The web app is static HTML and JavaScript, so it can be hosted anywhere for free.

Music. Each radar image is cut into 16 vertical strips. The brightness of a strip sets the pitch of a note, the change since the previous pass sets how loud it is, and its position sets left or right. Places that change sound different from places that stay the same.

Benefits and impact. People who are not radar experts can read a radar time series in seconds. Flood managers see open-water area and its trend even under monsoon cloud. Fire managers see where woody vegetation was really lost inside a fire perimeter. Teachers can use the stories and the sound in class. Everything is open source, and a new place is added by writing its coordinates into one file.

Validation and honesty. The fire result is checked against official fire perimeters that were not used in the detection. The app also shows a case where the method fails: the Big Grass Fire, a large grass fire that L-band radar barely sees, with an explanation why. Every place has a "Method and limits" section.

Tools and languages. Python (NumPy, h5py, Requests, pyproj, Pillow), JavaScript, HTML, CSS, MapLibre GL JS, Web Audio API, GitHub Pages.

Creativity. Change is not only drawn but also played as music, so it can be noticed by ear.

Use of SI. An SI assistant (Claude) wrote most of the code and drafted the texts; the idea and the decisions are mine. The app shows no SI-generated images or sound. The two demo videos use real footage of the app; their captions, cuts and music are SI-generated and carry a visible watermark.
